title: Why Open-Source RISC-V Chips Are Threatening Intel and ARM’s Decades-Long Monopoly — Engineering Cheat Sheet
subtitle: Modular, royalty-free ISA disrupting proprietary silicon dominance via open collaboration.
summary: RISC-V is an open-standard Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) that eliminates vendor lock-in and licensing fees by allowing developers to design custom, royalty-free processors. For software engineers, it represents a shift toward hardware-software co-design and democratized access to high-performance computing architectures.

key_concepts.name: Load-Store Architecture
key_concepts.detail: RISC-V follows a strictly load-store design, separating memory access from arithmetic instructions, which simplifies pipeline implementation, enhances clock speeds, and improves compiler optimization efficiency for modern silicon.

key_concepts.name: Modular ISA Design
key_concepts.detail: Unlike CISC, RISC-V uses a small base integer ISA (RV32I/RV64I) with optional standard extensions (M, A, F, D, C, V), allowing designers to include only necessary hardware logic.

key_concepts.name: Hardware-Software Co-design
key_concepts.detail: Engineers can add custom instructions for specific workloads—like AI inference or cryptography—without needing licensing approval, drastically reducing latency and power consumption for specialized high-compute applications.

code_cheatsheet.explanation: Compiles code for 64-bit RISC-V using the 'gc' extension set (General-purpose + Compressed instructions) and the lp64d ABI for double-precision float support.
Utilizes 'Spike', the official RISC-V ISA simulator, to execute and debug binary files in a virtual environment without needing physical FPGA hardware.

best_practices: Prioritize the base ISA (RV64IM) for maximum compatibility across common GCC/LLVM toolchains.
Leverage the 'C' (Compressed) extension to reduce binary size and cache footprint for embedded systems.
Utilize standard memory ordering models to ensure consistent multi-core cache coherency across different implementations.
Profile custom ISA extensions with cycle-accurate simulators before committing to hard silicon gates.

interview_qa.question: How does RISC-V’s open ISA differ from ARM’s licensing model, and what impact does this have on hardware development?
interview_qa.answer: ARM licenses their proprietary micro-architecture for a fee, restricting modifications to ensure standard performance. RISC-V provides an open specification, allowing companies to design custom chips with proprietary secret-sauce extensions without licensing fees, effectively commoditizing the base CPU logic.
